_what: Deliberately-distinct problem ids. Each entry is ONE adjudicated decision naming a SET of ids that are correctly separate from one another; problem_id_collision_gate suppresses every pair drawn from that set. This is the registration path PLA-449 asks for: a near-duplicate id is very often correct host or pathogen scoping, and a decision written down here stops the gate re-asking it every batch.
_how_to_add: Register only after ADJUDICATING the organisms, never to quiet the gate. State the reason in terms of the taxon or the scope the two entries actually cover -- not the id strings -- and cite where the ruling was made. An id pair that is genuinely one problem does NOT belong here; merge the ids instead.
_seeded: 2026-09-04, PLA-449. Nine entries transcribed from PLA-449's known-good list, one from PLA-448 s2 'Confirmed distinct -- do NOT merge'. Nothing else is registered: every other finding the gate reports is an OPEN decision.

carrot Alternaria dauci and Cercospora carotae on an Apiaceae, both seedborne; lemongrass Curvularia spp. on a Poaceae grass. The shared normalized name is an artifact of total parenthetical deletion on carrot's 'Leaf blight (Alternaria and Cercospora)', not a shared organism.

cilantro's entry is a DISEASE-VECTOR problem (beet leafhopper Circulifer tenellus vectoring aster yellows and beet curly top; its own record says the disease damage far outweighs the feeding). sage's are Eupteryx decemnotata and E. melissae, Lamiaceae-specialist direct feeders that vector nothing. Sharing one id would attach a vector ladder to a non-vector pest.

one pathogen species, Puccinia menthae, in host-specialized races that do not cross-infect. wsu_ext documents the race structure within the species ('Two principal types of races of P. menthae have been recognized. One type infects Native spearmint but not peppermint'). The direct mint-to-oregano cross-inoculation evidence is JOURNAL-ONLY (APS, 403 under every fetch path available) and is deliberately NOT relied on. Both display names read 'Mint rust' because psu_ext and rhs both call the disease that on oregano.

allium pink root (Setophoma terrestris) vs celery pink rot (Sclerotinia). MINTED BY BATCH 24: pink-root did not exist at the audit base 80519a28, so this pair is the first collision the gate caught that the 2026-09-03 audits could not have listed.

mulberry's is Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori (TAMU Plant Disease Handbook, mulberry), a mulberry-specific pathovar on a woody tree; edamame's `bacterial-blight` is P. savastanoi pv. glycinea on soybean. Same generic display name, different pathovars and hosts, the bacterial-spot / bacterial-spot-pruni shape. Registered as a PAIR, not a three-id set, so the open edamame/bean duplicate (PLA-448 s4a) stays unsuppressed.

mulberry's P. syringae pv. mori vs the beans' Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli + P. syringae pv. phaseolicola. The shared normalized key 'bacterial blight' is an artifact of total parenthetical deletion on the beans' 'Bacterial blights (common and halo)'. Registered as a PAIR for the same reason as above.

cherry's entry is two named Prunus borers (peachtree borer Synanthedon exitiosa, a clearwing moth at the crown, and American plum borer). mulberry's is an UNRESOLVED umbrella: the admissible literature (NCSU toolbox prose, TAMU) names no organism, UC IPM's mulberry page lists no borer, and the one US extension naming one (K-State MF2735, Dorcaschema wildii, a longhorn beetle; not catalog-admitted) is a different insect from either of cherry's. The shared key 'borer' is the parenthetical-deletion artifact on cherry's display name.

two crop-scoped umbrellas on unrelated hosts: persimmon's principal is Pseudocercospora diospyricola (UAEX Plant Health Clinic; Cercospora spp. per UF/IFAS HS1389) on Diospyros; lavender's one named organism is Septoria lavandulae on Lavandula. Same bare display name 'Leaf spot' by the same batch-25 rule (a genuine umbrella keeps the bare name); nothing about either ladder transfers.

lavender's id exists BECAUSE its organism is resolved narrower than the genus (P. nicotianae, dedicated WSU source; batch 25 s4). persimmon's is Phytophthora spp. (UC IPM persimmon page lists 'Phytophthora Root and Crown Rot' separately from Armillaria) and joins the roster's genus-level id alongside blueberry, raspberry and blackberry. The display names coincide ('Phytophthora root and crown rot', UC IPM's own title) because both name the genus; the ids differ because one pins a species.

celery early blight is Cercospora apii; the seven tomato, potato and tomatillo crops on `early-blight` carry Alternaria solani. UC IPM's celery early-blight page (read 2026-09-05) says it outright: 'do not confuse this disease with the early blight disease that occurs on tomato and potato, which is caused by an Alternaria species'. Celery's display name stays as authored because 'early blight' IS the celery-literature name (PLA-451); only the join key moved, on the bacterial-spot / bacterial-spot-pruni pattern.

celery late blight is Septoria apiicola; the six tomato and potato crops on `late-blight` carry Phytophthora infestans. UC IPM's celery late-blight page (read 2026-09-05): 'this disease is not the same as late blight of tomato and potato caused by Phytophthora infestans, which does not infect celery'. Same split, same reason as celery-early-blight (PLA-451).
